newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu charts vision of final peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu charts vision of final peace deal.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sketched on Wednesday a peace blueprint that appeared to give little ground to the Palestinians and vowed to keep Jerusalem united under Israeli control "for eternity".
At the same time he announced that more police would be stationed to tighten Israel's security grip on Arab East Jerusalem.

A senior government source said Netanyahu spelled out for the first time to his security cabinet his vision of a permanent peace settlement in which Israel would keep key areas in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
The prime minister laid out the plan, promptly condemned by Palestinians and Jewish settlers alike, as Israel marked the 30th anniversary of its capture of East Jerusalem.

"The main meaning of this victory is that Jerusalem will remain united and whole under Israeli sovereignty for eternity," Netanyahu, referring to the 1967 Middle East war, told parliament on "Jerusalem Day".
His spokesman issued a statement saying 400 extra Israeli police would be stationed permanently in East Jerusalem "to boost security and law and order in all of the city's neighbourhoods".
The PLO, which hopes to make East Jerusalem capital of a future Palestinian state, blasted the move.
"It is a decision to suppress and terrorise the Palestinian people in Jerusalem," Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, secretary general of the Palestinian cabinet, told Reuters.
Under the Netanyahu plan, Israel would keep full control of "Greater Jerusalem", including the Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements to the south, and the Jordan Valley, the source said.
Israel would also control other blocs of settlements in the West Bank as well as areas near the pre-1967 Middle East war border of the Jewish state and "vital roads", the source added.
"This is a blueprint for confrontation -- not a peace plan -- and an attempt to dictate a solution to the Palestinians," said Ahmed Tibi, an adviser to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
But the reference to settlement blocs sounded an alarm bell with Jewish settler leaders who fear some isolated outposts might be abandoned in a final peace deal with the PLO.

"The position of the Council of Jewish Settlements is that all settlements will remain in place and be developed," the group said in a statement. "A national government that does not uphold this principle will not last."

Netanyahu, who has pledged to expand existing settlements where some 135,000 Israelis now live, plunged Middle East peacemaking into crisis in March by sending bulldozers to start work on 6,500 homes for Jews in East Jerusalem.
Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem, including the walled Old City, after the 1967 war has never been recognised internationally.
Palestinians refuse to resume peace talks with Israel until construction is stopped at the hilltop site called Har Homa by Israelis and Jabal Abu Ghneim by Arabs.

"I would like to make clear again what is sometimes forgotten by gentiles and perhaps by us as well: we did not steal (Jerusalem) from any nation, faith or religion," Netanyahu told a special parliamentary session.
"Never in its history has Jerusalem been so open...or full of religious freedom as in the 30 years it has been under Israeli sovereignty."
Right-wing Israelis carrying Israeli flags marched through Arab areas of the city on Jerusalem Day. No serious violence was reported.
